CHF.Slab: The SNB counts five to six licensed fintech companies among SIC participants but names none of them. FINMA lists six FinTech licence holders. The match between the two lists is the open question, not whether anyone has taken a seat.
CHF.Policy line: Art 1b FinTech licence holders with a CHF payments business model can hold a sight deposit account at the SNB. The SNB's 2025 SIC report counts five to six of them as participants.

EUR.Slab: One nonbank is on a central bank's list. Paysera LT appears on the Bank of Lithuania's official TARGET participant list of 5 May 2026. The ECB's own annual report says no nonbank was connected at the end of 2025. ISX Financial announced Central Bank of Cyprus authorisation in October 2025 and is not shown live anywhere. The ECB publishes no list of its own.
EUR.Policy line: Nonbank PSPs can hold T2 and TIPS accounts from 6 October 2025 under ECB/2025/2 and Guideline ECB/2025/28. The original June 2025 date was postponed.

BRL.Slab: Brazil publishes the file and it reads in full. The central bank's list of active Pix participants dated 27 October 2026 shows Nu Pagamentos, PagSeguro, Stone, PicPay, Mercado Pago, dLocal, EBANX and Adyen do Brasil as direct participants with their own accounts. Wise Brasil is indirect. The list carries 900 rows and the central bank keeps only the current day's file at the published address.

CAD.State: Eligible, accounts opening with Real-Time Rail
CAD.Slab: A registered PSP can hold its own settlement account at the Bank of Canada for the Real-Time Rail. The rail is switching on in phases. Wealthsimple was approved in 2022 and has never used it. It reaches Lynx through Royal Bank of Canada today. The data names no sponsor bank for KOHO, Float or Paramount.
CAD.Policy line: The Bank of Canada's RTR access policy lets a registered PSP open its own settlement account, funded only through a Lynx participant. Wealthsimple was approved under it in October 2022. The policy page was last updated 31 July 2026.

CNY.State: Denied, with every wallet's money at the central bank
CNY.Slab: No payment company has a settlement seat in China. Every one of them has an account at the central bank anyway. Since 2019 client funds sit in a custody account at the PBOC and every transfer runs through a state clearing house. Lithuania's central bank lends nonbanks its seat. China's holds their client money in custody, at the central bank or a bank it approves, and routes every transfer through a state clearing house. Neither is a settlement seat.
CNY.Policy line: PBOC Order 2021 No. 1 requires client reserve funds to be deposited in full at the PBOC or a qualifying bank and transferred only through an approved clearing institution. In force 1 March 2021.

KRW.State: Unknown on paper, charter in practice
KRW.Slab: The Bank of Korea said in 2020 that a fintech could settle directly if it took on bank-equivalent obligations. None is on record doing it. Kakao, K bank and Toss took banking licences instead, and the payment apps still settle through banks for every transaction.
KRW.Policy line: Direct participation criteria for fintechs are known only from secondary reports. The three internet-only banks were licensed by the FSC in 2016, 2017 and 2021.

GBP.Slab: Wise was the first non-bank to settle Faster Payments in central bank money, through its own Bank of England settlement account, and the Bank publishes no count of who followed. Pay.UK lists 47 Faster Payments participants, about 15 of them payment companies, without saying which settle in their own account and which through a sponsor. Modulr says it has one, and no list confirms it.
GBP.Policy line: Nonbank payment institutions and e-money institutions have been eligible for settlement accounts since July 2017. No nonbank is on the high-value system as of the CHAPS list of 17 August 2026.

USD.Slab: No payment company settles on the Federal Reserve's books. Three novel-charter applicants have been approved since December 2022, all chartered institutions, and only Kraken Financial's account is live, Fedwire only. Every nonbank program rides a sponsor bank's master account, and the US sponsor bank list is the longest on this map.
USD.Policy line: Only legally eligible charters may apply. The payment account proposal of 20 May 2026 would set a balance limit, no interest and no intraday credit. Tier 3 decisions are paused.

MXN.Slab: Mexico publishes the list. Banxico's SPEI participants as of 23 September 2026 include 13 fintechs licensed as IFPEs with their own accounts, all of them drawn here. dLocal and EBANX are not on it.
MXN.Policy line: Circular 14/2017 as amended. No intraday credit or overdraft, end-of-day sweep to SIAC. Indirect participants are pushed to direct status above thresholds.

SGD.Slab: Licensed payment companies connect to FAST and PayNow themselves through an API gateway since February 2021. Whether any of them holds a settlement account at MAS is not stated in any MAS document read, so settlement is assumed to run through a bank. About eight nonbanks connect, including Wise, Grab and Singtel Dash.
SGD.Policy line: MAS opened direct FAST and PayNow participation to major payment institutions on 30 November 2020. The MEPS+ service agreement of 1 October 2021 governs who holds a settlement account.

rows.name: Lynx
rows.fn: Canada's system for large, time-critical payments like wires. Each payment settles on the Bank of Canada's books as it goes, through the business day.
rows.chain: 16 participants, the Bank of Canada and 15 financial institutions. More than 50 others reach it through a participant.

rows.name: ACSS
rows.fn: Canada's system for everyday payments, like direct deposits, pre-authorized debits, cheques and Interac debit. A day of payments settles on the Bank of Canada's books the next business day.
rows.chain: Direct clearers settle their net amount at the Bank of Canada. Everyone else clears through a direct clearer.

rows.name: Real-Time Rail
rows.fn: Canada's new real-time payment system, switching on in phases. Registered payment companies can hold their own settlement account at the Bank of Canada.
rows.chain: Direct participants at launch. Interac e-Transfer clearing and settlement moves over next. A payment company's account is funded through a Lynx participant.

rows.name: Visa and Mastercard in Canada
rows.fn: The card networks for Canadian credit and debit cards. They set the rules and carry the payment between card issuers and acquirers, then settle through their settlement banks.
rows.chain: The Bank of Canada oversees VisaNet and Mastercard's clearing and settlement systems. Settlement runs once a day through the networks' settlement banks, as card networks usually work.

rows.name: Singapore local banks (DBS, OCBC, UOB)
rows.fn: Commercial banks with their own settlement accounts in MEPS+ at the Monetary Authority of Singapore. They are direct FAST and PayNow participants and hold the accounts most people and companies in Singapore use.

rows.name: Hong Kong licensed banks (HSBC, BOCHK, Hang Seng)
rows.fn: Every licensed bank in Hong Kong, including the Bank of China (Hong Kong), known as BOCHK, must be a direct participant in HKD CHATS and FPS, with its own settlement account at the HKMA. HSBC is also the settlement institution for US dollar CHATS in Hong Kong.

rows.name: Indian PSP banks (SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank)
rows.fn: Banks that are UPI members and connect apps to UPI. Third-party apps such as Google Pay and PhonePe do not connect to UPI themselves. They ride on these PSP banks, and the money sits in customers' own bank accounts.

rows.name: Brazil large banks (Itaú, Bradesco, Banco do Brasil, Caixa, Santander)
rows.fn: Mandatory direct participants in Pix, because any institution with more than 500,000 active accounts must join. Each settles Pix payments on its own account at the Banco Central do Brasil.

PLAIN.P010: The US central bank, providing final settlement for US dollars through Fedwire. Master accounts go to insured depository institutions, with novel charters considered case by case.
PLAIN.P011: The instant payment rail operated by the Federal Reserve. Participant banks hold customer funds and settle FedNow payments in central bank money at the Fed.
PLAIN.P012: A private large-value US dollar system run by The Clearing House that nets payments continuously and settles positions through Fedwire. Participants are licensed banks, and those without a Fed account prefund through another participant.
PLAIN.P013: A private instant payment rail run by The Clearing House. Participant banks prefund a joint account at the Federal Reserve, so each payment settles in central bank money.
PLAIN.P014: A settlement system for foreign exchange trades that pays both currency legs at the same time. It settles through accounts at the central banks of each currency it covers.
PLAIN.P015: A Wyoming special purpose depository institution with a limited purpose Federal Reserve account. It sells custody and US dollar settlement to institutional clients and settles directly at the Fed.
PLAIN.P016: A Wyoming special purpose depository institution without a Federal Reserve master account, so it has no direct path to central bank settlement for US dollars.
PLAIN.P017: A large US bank that provides dollar clearing and correspondent accounts to other banks, settling at the Federal Reserve. It also runs Kinexys Digital Payments, a blockchain-based deposit network.
PLAIN.P018: A global bank offering 24/7 US dollar clearing to other banks from its own Federal Reserve master account and CHIPS membership. It also holds local scheme memberships in its own name, including Lynx in Canada.
PLAIN.P019: A US bank that acts as a dollar correspondent for other banks, settling their payments through its own account at the Federal Reserve.
PLAIN.P020: A US sponsor bank for fintech programs such as Affirm, Coinbase and Circle. It holds customer funds in for-benefit-of accounts and settles at the Federal Reserve.
PLAIN.P021: A US sponsor bank for fintech programs that settles at the Federal Reserve. It works with Cross River on Visa's USDC stablecoin settlement pilot.
PLAIN.P022: A US sponsor bank for fintech programs, including those run through Synapse. It holds customer funds in for-benefit-of accounts and settles at the Federal Reserve.
PLAIN.P023: A nationally chartered, developer-focused sponsor bank behind fintechs such as Mercury and Brex. It holds customer funds and settles directly at the Federal Reserve.
PLAIN.P024: A US sponsor bank for prepaid and card programs and Marqeta's original issuing bank. It holds program funds and settles at the Federal Reserve.
PLAIN.P025: A US sponsor bank for payments and card programs. It holds funds in pooled accounts with a record for each card, plus custodial deposits kept off its balance sheet, and settles at the Federal Reserve.
PLAIN.P026: A small Kansas state bank that runs a fintech sponsor model, holding program funds and settling at the Federal Reserve.
PLAIN.P027: A US sponsor bank for fintechs including Wise and Crypto.com. It holds customer funds and settles at the Federal Reserve.
PLAIN.P028: Banking-as-a-service software that connects fintechs to sponsor banks. It does not settle payments itself. The sponsor bank holds customer funds and handles settlement.
PLAIN.P029: Banking-as-a-service software that connects fintechs to several sponsor banks. The sponsor banks hold customer funds and handle settlement.
PLAIN.P031: A software company whose Interlace platform lets banks run embedded finance programs. The client bank holds customer funds and handles settlement.
PLAIN.P032: A card issuer processor and program manager. Issuing banks hold the charter, the balance sheet and customer funds, and they handle settlement.
PLAIN.P033: An issuer processor and core banking platform owned by SoFi, now presented as SoFi Tech Solutions. The issuing bank holds customer funds and handles settlement.
PLAIN.P034: An issuer processor and core banking platform used across many currencies. The issuing bank holds customer funds and handles settlement.
PLAIN.P035: A processor for credit, prepaid and debit card programs, now owned by Euronet. The issuing bank holds customer funds and handles settlement.
PLAIN.P036: Visa's push payment service, sending funds to cards over VisaNet and to accounts through ACH and RTP partners. Settlement runs through settlement banks, and USDC settlement is live via Cross River and Lead Bank.
PLAIN.P037: Mastercard's cross-border push payment network, settling through settlement banks. A pilot with the Eurosystem's TIPS instant system tests cross-currency payments settled in central bank money.
PLAIN.P038: A member-owned messaging cooperative that carries payment instructions between banks, with gpi tracking. It moves no money itself. Settlement happens across members' correspondent accounts. It also provides messaging for Canada's Lynx.
PLAIN.P039: Issuer of the USDC and EURC stablecoins and operator of Circle Payments Network. Most USDC reserves sit in a BlackRock-managed fund held at BNY, with the rest in cash at large global banks.
PLAIN.P040: Stripe's stablecoin orchestration and issuance business. It holds money transmitter licences across US states and an e-money licence in Luxembourg, and relies on partner banks for reserves and settlement.
PLAIN.P041: A US national trust bank that holds digital assets and issues USDPT, Western Union's stablecoin. Reserves backing the stablecoin are held with custodians.
PLAIN.P042: A consumer money transfer company that settles through correspondent banks today and is testing its USDPT stablecoin for agent settlement. It holds settlement assets on its own balance sheet, restricted to meeting settlement obligations.
PLAIN.P043: Euronet's cross-border payout network, delivering funds to bank accounts and mobile wallets through partner banks. Citi routes wallet payouts through it.
PLAIN.P044: The UK central bank, providing final settlement for CHAPS, Faster Payments and Bacs. Nonbank payment companies can hold their own settlement accounts there.
PLAIN.P045: A UK e-money firm that connects directly to Faster Payments. A settling bank generally handles settlement, though the company says it holds its own Bank of England settlement account. Customer funds are safeguarded.
PLAIN.P046: A Luxembourg bank selling accounts, local clearing and foreign exchange to payment companies. It reaches T2 for euros and holds accounts at several central banks, keeping most client funds there or in government bonds.
PLAIN.P047: The European Central Bank, providing final settlement for euros through T2 and the TIPS instant system. Nonbank payment companies can now hold their own T2 and TIPS accounts.
PLAIN.P048: A private euro clearing company running RT1 for instant payments and STEP2 for batch payments. Both are fully backed by funds held in TARGET2, so payments settle in central bank money.
PLAIN.P050: A cross-border payout network that delivers funds to bank accounts and wallets through partner banks and direct bank connections. US payouts run through a large US bank.
PLAIN.P051: A cross-border payout network holding e-money licences in the UK and EU and US state money transmitter licences. It connects to rails technically and uses partner banks to pay out and settle.
PLAIN.P052: A global payments company that reaches local clearing through partner banks and its own licensed entities. Its UK payments run through ClearBank, and some US flows through Evolve.
PLAIN.P053: Singapore's central bank, providing final settlement for Singapore dollars in MEPS+, its real-time gross settlement system. Nonbanks that join FAST settle through banks rather than their own MEPS+ account.
PLAIN.P054: Japan's domestic interbank clearing system, with net positions settled at the Bank of Japan. Wise Payments Japan is the only funds transfer provider admitted and holds a restricted Bank of Japan current account.
PLAIN.P055: Operator of UPI, India's instant payment system. Only payment service provider banks connect directly, and nonbank apps ride on them. Net positions settle at the Reserve Bank of India.
PLAIN.P056: A project to link domestic instant payment systems across countries, run by an entity set up by participating central banks. Settlement happens in each member's instant payment system, and it is not yet live.
PLAIN.P057: The Arab Monetary Fund's multi-currency cross-border clearing and settlement platform. Each currency settles through a settlement bank, with Standard Chartered handling euros.
PLAIN.P058: The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, run with Afreximbank. It clears instant payments across Africa and settles net positions daily in local currencies through participating central banks, with Afreximbank handling the hard-currency leg.
PLAIN.P059: Safaricom's mobile money wallet, used for last-mile payouts in Kenya and Ethiopia. M-Pesa to M-Pesa payments stay on Safaricom's books. The money behind balances sits in a trust fund at commercial banks and in government securities.
PLAIN.P060: A pan-African payments company handling collections and payouts across several African currencies. It settles through partner banks and has obtained a Nigerian microfinance bank licence.
PLAIN.P061: Brazil's central bank, which owns and operates the Pix instant payment system and the SPI settlement system. Banks and payment institutions can join directly or indirectly.
PLAIN.P062: A payments company handling pay-ins and payouts in emerging markets. It is a Central Bank of Brazil payment institution with direct access to Pix, and uses local acquirers elsewhere.
PLAIN.P063: A collection agent that lets global merchants accept local payments in Latin America without a local entity. It settles through partner banks and acquirers.
PLAIN.P064: A UK bank providing foreign exchange and payouts in hard-to-reach currencies to banks, fintechs and development organisations. It takes the currency position itself, settling sterling at the Bank of England and other currencies through partner banks.
PLAIN.P065: Visa's foreign exchange and multi-currency account service, sold by API to banks, fintechs and currency brokers. It collects, converts and pays out through partner bank liquidity providers, holding client funds in safeguarded bank accounts.
PLAIN.P066: A global bank providing US dollar correspondent services through its own Federal Reserve account and CHIPS membership. It offers multi-currency clearing for banks and payment companies and joins China's CIPS directly for renminbi.
PLAIN.P067: A global bank providing US dollar correspondent services through its own Federal Reserve account and CHIPS membership. It holds local clearing memberships across emerging markets and is the euro settlement bank for Buna.
PLAIN.P068: The UK operator and standards body for Faster Payments, Bacs and cheque image clearing. It sets rules and admits participants, and payments settle at the Bank of England in deferred net batches several times a day.
PLAIN.P069: Mexico's central bank, which owns and operates SPEI, a real-time gross settlement system on its own books. Nonbanks such as fintechs, brokerages and money transmitters can join SPEI directly.
PLAIN.P070: China's cross-border renminbi clearing and settlement system, backed by the People's Bank of China. Direct participants settle on CIPS accounts, with final settlement onshore through CNAPS.
PLAIN.P071: A consumer remittance app that settles through funding and disbursement partner banks, wallets and cash pickup networks. It often pays out before customer funds clear, and third-party financial institutions hold customer funds.
PLAIN.P072: PayPal's money transfer service, sending to bank accounts, mobile wallets and cash pickup. The group settles through its own licensed bank in Luxembourg for the EU and through partner banks elsewhere.
PLAIN.P073: A UK clearing bank that sells agency banking and scheme access to fintechs, e-money firms and banks. It holds sterling client funds at the Bank of England and euro client funds at the Dutch central bank and the ECB.
PLAIN.P074: A creator and gig marketplace that offers operators a white-label neobank. Balances sit in pooled for-benefit-of accounts at partner banks, withdrawals run through Cross River, and dollars can convert to USDT stablecoin.
PLAIN.P075: Program manager for the Whop Card, a Visa card issued by Third National under Rain's program and secured by USDT stablecoin collateral. Rain settles daily with Visa.
PLAIN.P076: A US consumer neobank whose debit and credit cards are issued by The Bancorp Bank and Stride Bank. Those banks hold member deposits in omnibus accounts and handle settlement.
PLAIN.P101: Australia's central bank, providing final settlement for Australian dollars in RITS. NPP participants settle each payment in real time on their Exchange Settlement Accounts.
PLAIN.P102: Owner and operator of Australia's New Payments Platform, formed by merging BPAY, eftpos and NPP Australia. Payments settle at the Reserve Bank of Australia.
PLAIN.P103: An Australian licensed bank that provides settlement and processing services to banks and payment companies through its Reserve Bank of Australia account. Banking Circle agreed to acquire it.
PLAIN.P104: Hong Kong's central bank, providing final settlement for Hong Kong dollars on banks' settlement accounts. Each FPS payment settles individually on a ledger account paired with the bank's real-time gross settlement account.
PLAIN.P105: Developer and operator of Hong Kong's Faster Payment System, running 24/7 in Hong Kong dollars and renminbi. Hong Kong dollar payments settle at the HKMA and renminbi payments through the renminbi clearing bank.
PLAIN.P106: The UAE central bank, providing final settlement for dirhams. It owns, hosts and manages UAEFTS, the country's real-time gross settlement system.
PLAIN.P107: Operator of Aani, the UAE instant payment platform launched under the central bank's Financial Infrastructure Transformation programme. Participants settle at the Central Bank of the UAE.
PLAIN.P108: A UAE exchange house offering outward personal remittances and foreign exchange through its branch network, a common route for the UAE to India corridor. It settles through partner and correspondent banks.
PLAIN.P109: Saudi Arabia's central bank, providing final settlement for riyals. SARIE is its real-time gross settlement system and settles linked systems, including the sarie instant payment service.

PLAIN.P111: The Philippine central bank, which owns and operates PhilPaSSplus, the only peso real-time gross settlement system. It settles the InstaPay and PESONet clearing systems.
PLAIN.P112: The payment system management body that governs the InstaPay and PESONet schemes in the Philippines. Participants settle at Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.
PLAIN.P113: A Philippine mobile wallet operated by Mynt through G-Xchange, used as a last-mile payout for inbound remittances. Philippine rules require its e-money to be backed by bank deposits or government securities.

PLAIN.P115: Owner and operator of Korea's retail payment systems, including electronic banking and open banking. Member banks' net positions settle at the Bank of Korea.
PLAIN.P116: Indonesia's central bank, providing final settlement for rupiah through BI-RTGS and BI-FAST. Well-capitalised nonbanks can join BI-FAST, but direct participants must also be BI-RTGS participants.
PLAIN.P117: South Africa's central bank, providing final settlement for rand through SAMOS, the real-time gross settlement system for banks and financial institutions. SAMOS is being overhauled.
PLAIN.P118: Operator of South Africa's national clearing infrastructure and PayShap, the instant payment rail, formerly known as BankservAfrica. Participant banks settle at the South African Reserve Bank.
PLAIN.P119: Switzerland's central bank, providing final settlement for francs. As SIC system manager it keeps participants' sight deposit accounts and sets admission rules.
PLAIN.P120: Operator of the SIC platform, Switzerland's real-time gross settlement and instant payment system. Participants contract with both the Swiss National Bank and SIX, and settle on sight deposit accounts at the central bank.
PLAIN.P201: A US sponsor bank that has long served Chime, holding member funds in omnibus accounts and settling at the Federal Reserve. Chime agreed to acquire it, to become Chime Bank N.A.
PLAIN.P202: A US sponsor bank for Chime and other fintech programs. It holds member deposits in omnibus accounts and settles at the Federal Reserve.
PLAIN.P203: Chime's planned bank charter through its pending acquisition of Stride Bank. With regulatory approval, Chime Bank N.A. would hold member funds and settle directly at the Federal Reserve. Nothing is live yet.
PLAIN.P301: India's central bank, providing final settlement for rupees on its own books. Prepaid instrument issuers, card networks and white-label ATM operators can join RTGS and NEFT with accounts at the central bank.
PLAIN.P401: A consumer and small business money transfer product that owns the customer relationship and pricing. Its own licensed payment entities hold the scheme seats and safeguard customer funds.
PLAIN.P402: A UK clearing bank whose agency banking lends its Bank of England settlement account and Faster Payments, CHAPS and Bacs access to e-money firms and fintechs. Clients, including Airwallex, settle on ClearBank's account.
PLAIN.P403: Banking Circle lends its T2 access to payment companies and acquirers, giving them euro accounts and SEPA and SEPA Instant reach. Clients settle on Banking Circle's account at the ECB.
PLAIN.P404: Western Union's agent cash payout network, where recipients collect cash at retail agent locations. Banks and other money transfer operators rent it for cash delivery, and Western Union advances funds to agents.
PLAIN.P405: A merchant acquirer and payment company holding its own Exchange Settlement Account at the Reserve Bank of Australia, the only nonbank payment company on the RITS list.
PLAIN.P406: MercadoLibre's wallet and payments arm. It is a direct participant in Pix in Brazil and SPEI in Mexico, settling on its own accounts at both central banks.
PLAIN.P407: Japan's central bank, providing final settlement for yen on current accounts, where Zengin net positions settle. Funds transfer providers are admitted case by case, with Wise Payments Japan the first.
PLAIN.P501: China's central bank, providing final settlement for onshore renminbi through CNAPS. It holds every nonbank payment institution's client reserve funds in a central custody account, with transfers only through approved clearing houses.
PLAIN.P502: A state-backed clearing house for online payments by nonbank payment institutions in China. These institutions clear bank-linked payments through NetsUnion or UnionPay instead of directly with banks, and settle at the People's Bank of China.
PLAIN.P503: An internet-only bank launched by the parent of Korea's Toss payment app. The fintech took a bank charter rather than a nonbank seat and settles at the Bank of Korea as a bank.
PLAIN.P504: A Lithuanian e-money firm that is a direct participant in the Lithuanian component of TARGET, an early nonbank to settle euros directly in central bank money. Customer funds are safeguarded.
PLAIN.P505: A Cyprus e-money firm authorised by the Central Bank of Cyprus for T2 access, which would let it settle euros in central bank money. Customer funds are safeguarded.
PLAIN.P506: The Bank of Lithuania's payment gateway. It lends the central bank's own TARGET participation to e-money firms and payment companies, giving them TIPS, RT1 and SEPA reach without a commercial sponsor bank.
PLAIN.P508: Singapore's retail instant transfer scheme and its PayNow addressing service, owned through the Association of Banks in Singapore. Licensed major payment institutions can connect directly, while settlement runs through banks in MEPS+.
PLAIN.P509: A Mexican merchant acquirer and payments app licensed as an e-money firm. It is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico.
PLAIN.P510: A Mexican consumer account app licensed as an e-money firm. It is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico.
PLAIN.P511: Mexican payments infrastructure licensed as an e-money firm and a direct SPEI participant at the Banco de Mexico. It also provides SPEI access to fintechs.
PLAIN.P512: A consumer wallet anchored in Oxxo's retail network and licensed as an e-money firm in Mexico. It is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico.
PLAIN.P513: A Mexican consumer account app licensed as an e-money firm. It joins SPEI directly and settles on its own account at the Banco de Mexico.
PLAIN.P514: PayPal's Mexican e-money firm. It is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico, with client funds backed by liquid reserves.
PLAIN.P515: A Mexican e-money firm that is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico. Client funds are backed by reserves under e-money rules.
PLAIN.P516: A Mexican e-money firm that is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico. Client funds are backed by reserves under e-money rules.
PLAIN.P517: A Mexican e-money firm offering digital deposits and payments. It is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico.
PLAIN.P518: A Mexican e-money firm that is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico. Client funds are backed by reserves under e-money rules.
PLAIN.P519: A Mexican e-money firm that is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico. Client funds are backed by reserves under e-money rules.
PLAIN.P520: A Mexican e-money firm that is a direct SPEI participant, settling on its own account at the Banco de Mexico. Client funds are backed by reserves under e-money rules.
PLAIN.P521: Nubank's payment institution in Brazil, required to participate in Pix directly. It settles on its own account at the Central Bank of Brazil through the SPI.
PLAIN.P522: A Brazilian payment institution required to participate in Pix directly. It settles on its own account at the Central Bank of Brazil through the SPI, with client funds kept segregated.
PLAIN.P523: A Brazilian merchant acquirer's payment institution and direct participant in Pix. It settles on its own account at the Central Bank of Brazil through the SPI.
PLAIN.P524: A Brazilian wallet and direct participant in Pix, settling on its own account at the Central Bank of Brazil through the SPI. PicPay Bank participates separately as a bank.
PLAIN.P525: Adyen's Brazilian payment institution and direct participant in Pix. It settles on its own account at the Central Bank of Brazil through the SPI.
PLAIN.C101: Canada's high-value payment system for large, time-critical payments like wires. Each payment settles individually on the Bank of Canada's books in real time through the business day.
PLAIN.C102: Canada's system for everyday payments such as direct deposits, pre-authorized debits, cheques and Interac debit. Each day's payments settle on the Bank of Canada's books the next business day.
PLAIN.C103: Canada's new real-time payment system, switching on in phases. Registered payment companies can hold their own settlement account at the Bank of Canada, giving them direct access to central bank settlement.
PLAIN.C104: Visa and Mastercard as the card networks for Canadian credit and debit cards. They set the rules, carry payments between card issuers and acquirers, and settle through their settlement banks.
PLAIN.P001: Canada's central bank. Every Canadian dollar payment becomes final on its books, through Lynx, ACSS and the new Real-Time Rail.
PLAIN.P002: Runs Canada's payment systems, Lynx, ACSS and Real-Time Rail, and decides who can join them.
PLAIN.P003: Bank-owned network behind debit and e-Transfer. It carries the payment between banks, and the banks settle with each other.
PLAIN.P004: Settles in Lynx on behalf of its member credit unions.
PLAIN.P005: A trust company with its own Bank of Canada account in ACSS. Also the bank behind many Canadian fintech programs.
PLAIN.P006: Investing and money app. Reaches Lynx through RBC today. Approved for its own Real-Time Rail account, not yet used.
PLAIN.P007: Money app and Payments Canada member. Settles through a sponsor bank today.
PLAIN.P008: Corporate cards and spend management. Payments Canada member, settles through a sponsor bank today.
PLAIN.P009: Pay-by-bank for merchants. Payments Canada member, settles through a bank today.
PLAIN.P030: Software that connects fintechs to sponsor banks. In Canada it works through National Bank. Holds no money.
PLAIN.P507: Canada's largest bank and a Lynx participant. Wealthsimple reaches Lynx through it.
PLAIN.P049: Global money transfers and accounts. Holds its own central bank accounts in the UK and Japan and connects directly to several national systems. Uses banks elsewhere, including in Canada.

CAD.name: Canada
CAD.line: One operator runs the core systems, one bank-owned network runs debit and e-Transfer, and payments between banks settle at the Bank of Canada.

dom: Payments Canada writes the rules for the core systems. Interac, the bank-owned domestic network, sets the rules for debit and e-Transfer. Card networks set their own.

Wires go through Lynx, the high-value payment system, and payroll, bill payments and cheques go through ACSS, the batch system. Everyday transfers go through Interac e-Transfer, which settles through Lynx. Interac debit settles through ACSS. Real-Time Rail, a new instant payment system, is switching on in phases.
Banks and credit unions hold deposits, and many credit unions settle through a central. Fintechs hold customer funds in safeguarded accounts at a bank or trust company.
Payments between banks settle at the Bank of Canada. Wires in Lynx settle one by one through the day, and batch payments in ACSS settle as a net amount the next business day.
The Bank of Canada oversees the core systems, Interac and the card networks, and supervises payment service providers. Banks answer to their prudential regulator.
xb: Correspondent banks agree terms bank to bank, and Swift sets the message standard. Card networks and global payment companies run their own rules.

Big banks send through correspondent accounts abroad. Global payment companies collect in Canada and pay out locally elsewhere. US dollar items between Canadian institutions clear through their own exchange, run by Payments Canada.
United States Bulk Exchange at Payments Canada
The sending bank holds the funds, then its correspondent abroad. With a global payment company, the company holds them in safeguarded accounts at banks.

Each currency settles at its own central bank, and US dollar items exchanged in Canada settle through correspondent banks in New York. Large FX trades settle both sides at once through CLS, the FX settlement system.

Each bank answers for its own leg under its home regulator. Payment companies are supervised by the Bank of Canada, register with FINTRAC, the financial intelligence unit, as money service businesses, and are licensed abroad.

CAD.stablecoin: A new federal Stablecoin Act puts fiat-backed stablecoin issuers under Bank of Canada registration and supervision, with regulations still being drafted. Until those are in place, stablecoins are mainly a cross-border option, and the draft rules would also bring payment companies using prescribed stablecoins under the Retail Payment Activities Act.
sources: Payments Canada, retail batch system (ACSS, USBE)
Bank of Canada, Overview of Lynx
Bank of Canada, systems it oversees
Bank of Canada, retail payments supervision

USD.name: United States
USD.line: The Fed and the big banks each run their own rails side by side, and thousands of banks and sponsor banks hold the money.

dom: The Fed sets rules for its own services. The Clearing House, owned by big banks, sets rules for CHIPS, its high-value system, and RTP, its instant system. Nacha writes the ACH rules and card networks set their own.

Wires go through Fedwire, the Fed's high-value system, or CHIPS. Payroll and bills go through ACH, run by the Fed and The Clearing House. Instant payments go through FedNow or RTP, and person-to-person goes through Zelle.
Banks and credit unions hold deposits. Only they can hold a Fed master account, so most fintechs hold customer funds at a sponsor bank.

Payments between banks settle in Federal Reserve accounts. Fedwire and FedNow settle each payment as it goes, CHIPS and RTP settle against prefunded joint accounts at the New York Fed, and ACH and cards settle as net amounts.

The Fed runs its own systems and supervises CHIPS, which is designated systemically important. Banks answer to federal or state regulators. Money transmitters register with FinCEN, the financial intelligence unit, and are licensed state by state.
xb: Correspondent banks agree terms bank to bank, and Swift sets the message standard. Card networks and global payment companies run their own rules.
US banks clear dollars for banks around the world, which makes them the end point of most cross-border chains. Global payment and remittance companies run their own networks.
Correspondent banks hold accounts for foreign banks, and global payment companies hold funds at partner banks.
Dollars settle at the Fed, usually through CHIPS or Fedwire, the two high-value systems. Large FX trades settle both sides at once through CLS, the FX settlement system the Fed supervises.
Each bank answers for its own leg under its home regulator. Remittance providers register with FinCEN, the financial intelligence unit, and hold state money transmitter licences.

USD.stablecoin: The GENIUS Act set a federal framework for payment stablecoins, with one-to-one reserves and issuers supervised by federal bank regulators, the OCC for nonbanks, or a similar state regime. Dollar stablecoins such as USDC are a cross-border option that moves outside the bank rails and meets them only when tokens are minted or redeemed.
sources: Fed, interest on RTP joint account

GBP.name: United Kingdom
GBP.line: The central bank runs both the real-time gross settlement ledger and the CHAPS high-value system, and regulated non-bank payment firms can hold their own settlement accounts at the Bank of England.

dom: The Bank of England sets the rules for CHAPS, the high-value payment system, and for its real-time gross settlement service. Pay.UK sets the scheme rules for Faster Payments, Bacs and cheque imaging, and card networks set their own. The FCA authorises payment and e-money firms and writes their conduct rules.

Banks and authorised payment firms send payments as direct participants or through a sponsor. Faster Payments carries instant payments around the clock, Bacs carries Direct Debits and Direct Credits in batches, and CHAPS carries high-value payments.

Customer money sits as deposits at banks. Payment and e-money firms must safeguard customer funds by segregating them or covering them with insurance or a guarantee. Settlement participants hold reserves in settlement accounts at the Bank of England.

All sterling systems settle in central bank money in the Bank of England's real-time gross settlement service. CHAPS, the high-value system, settles each payment one by one in real time. Faster Payments settles net three times a business day against prefunded balances, while Bacs, cheque imaging, LINK and Visa settle net on scheduled cycles.

The Bank of England supervises systemically important payment systems recognised by HM Treasury, including Faster Payments, Bacs, LINK, Visa Europe and Mastercard Europe, and oversees CHAPS on a non-statutory basis. The Payment Systems Regulator covers competition and access, and its functions are moving into the FCA.
xb: Cross-border messages follow Swift standards, with CHAPS, the high-value system, now on ISO 20022. Correspondent agreements and card network rules set the terms for each corridor.
Large banks move most cross-border value through correspondent banking over Swift. Global payment firms collect and pay out locally in each currency. Card networks handle cross-border card spending.
Correspondent banks hold balances for each other in nostro and vostro accounts. Global payment firms hold safeguarded customer balances at banks in each market.

The sterling leg of a cross-border payment settles in CHAPS, the high-value system, across the Bank of England's settlement accounts. For foreign exchange, CLS settles both currency legs payment-versus-payment and funds its sterling position as a CHAPS direct participant.

The Federal Reserve leads oversight of CLS, the FX settlement system, and the Bank of England supervises it in the UK as a recognised payment system. The FCA supervises UK payment firms, and each foreign leg falls under its local regulator.

GBP.stablecoin: Stablecoins are an emerging cross-border option, not a mainstream rail. The FCA is bringing UK stablecoin issuance and custody into regulation, and the Bank of England is finalising a regime for sterling systemic stablecoins.
sources: BoE, RTGS and CHAPS service description

EUR.name: Euro area
EUR.line: Euro area countries share one currency, one central bank settlement platform and one set of SEPA payment rules, and licensed nonbank payment firms can now settle in central bank money.

dom: EU law sets the baseline, including the Instant Payments Regulation that requires payment providers to offer euro instant transfers and payee name checks. The European Payments Council writes the rulebooks for the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA), covering credit transfers, instant transfers and direct debits.

Banks and licensed payment and e-money firms send SEPA payments through clearing houses, the largest being EBA Clearing with STEP2 for bulk payments and RT1 for instant payments. Cards run on Visa and Mastercard alongside national card schemes in a few countries.

Customer money sits at banks and payment and e-money firms, which hold settlement balances at their national central bank. Nonbank firms can hold accounts in T2 and TIPS, the Eurosystem settlement services, for settlement only, with capped balances and no intraday credit.

T2, the Eurosystem's real-time gross settlement system, settles large payments and acts as settlement agent for clearing houses such as STEP2 and EURO1, which net and then settle in central bank money. TIPS, the Eurosystem's instant settlement service, settles instant payments one by one around the clock, either directly or through RT1.

The ECB and the national central banks oversee payment systems, with the ECB as lead overseer for most systemically important ones such as T2, EURO1 and STEP2-T. Card and payment schemes fall under the Eurosystem's oversight framework for electronic payments.
xb: Within the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA), cross-border euro payments follow the same European Payments Council rules as domestic ones. Outside SEPA, banks follow Swift standards and correspondent agreements, and a one-leg-out instant scheme covers transfers with one end outside SEPA.

Inside SEPA a cross-border euro payment moves like a domestic one, through EBA Clearing's STEP2 and RT1 or the Eurosystem's TIPS. Outside SEPA, correspondent banks and money transfer firms carry the payment over Swift. TIPS also converts Swedish krona and Danish krone payments into euro, and a link to UPI, India's instant payment system, is being built.

Correspondent banks hold euro accounts for foreign banks and settle through their own central bank accounts. Foreign banks can be reached in T2, the Eurosystem settlement system, through a direct participant.

Euro legs settle in T2, the Eurosystem's real-time gross settlement system, through correspondent banks. CLS settles the euro side of FX trades payment versus payment, removing the risk that one side pays and the other does not.

The ECB has primary responsibility for euro settlement in CLS, the FX settlement system, while the US Federal Reserve leads CLS oversight overall. Eurosystem oversight also covers correspondent banks.

EUR.stablecoin: Euro and other stablecoins are regulated as e-money tokens under MiCA, the EU crypto-asset regulation, and can only be issued by authorised banks and e-money firms. They are an emerging cross-border option but remain small next to SEPA and correspondent banking.
sources: Eurosystem policy on nonbank PSP access

AUD.name: Australia
AUD.line: The Reserve Bank owns and runs the single settlement system, RITS, which settles NPP instant payments one by one around the clock, while an industry body and a member-owned operator run most clearing.

dom: The Reserve Bank's Payments System Board sets payments policy and can designate systems and impose standards, including on card interchange and surcharging. AusPayNet, the industry body, writes clearing rules, and Australian Payments Plus sets scheme rules for NPP (the instant payment system), eftpos and BPAY.

Banks and other deposit-takers send payments over several rails. NPP, the New Payments Platform, carries real-time account payments around the clock, BECS carries batch direct entry payments, card networks carry card payments, and large payments travel as Swift messages in HVCS, the high-value clearing system.

Customer money sits in deposit accounts at authorised deposit-taking institutions, mostly the large banks. Institutions settle in Exchange Settlement Accounts at the Reserve Bank, open to deposit-takers, non-bank payment providers with clearing obligations and licensed clearing facilities. Smaller institutions often settle through an agent.

RITS, owned and run by the Reserve Bank, settles high-value payments one by one in real time across Exchange Settlement Accounts. Its Fast Settlement Service settles each NPP payment individually around the clock. Direct entry, cheque and card obligations are netted and settled in batches through the Low Value Settlement Service.

APRA supervises deposit-takers, and its non-objection is needed before one gets its own settlement account. The Reserve Bank oversees payment infrastructure against international standards. ASIC, the corporate regulator, licenses financial services firms and AUSTRAC, the financial intelligence unit, supervises anti-money laundering compliance.
xb: Swift sets the messaging standard and CLS, the FX settlement system, sets the rules for settling foreign exchange. The AUD leg travels through HVCS, the high-value clearing system, and the financial intelligence unit requires remitters to register and report international transfers.

Most cross-border payments run through correspondent banking, where a foreign bank instructs an Australian bank that sends the payment through HVCS, the high-value clearing system. Global payment companies and remitters collect abroad and pay out over domestic rails such as NPP, the instant payment system.
Foreign banks hold AUD in accounts at Australian correspondent banks, which hold Exchange Settlement Accounts at the Reserve Bank. Payment companies usually keep customer funds at banks.

The AUD leg settles one by one in RITS, the Reserve Bank's settlement system, once the high-value payment message arrives over Swift. FX trades involving AUD can settle payment-versus-payment through CLS, which RITS supports.

Each bank and payment provider is accountable for its own sanctions and anti-money laundering checks and reports transfers to AUSTRAC, the financial intelligence unit. APRA supervises the banks carrying the flows and the Reserve Bank oversees RITS as infrastructure.

AUD.stablecoin: Treasury's draft payments licensing reforms treat payment stablecoins as tokenised stored value, with the provider holding an Australian financial services licence. A few AUD stablecoins already operate under licences and regulator relief lets intermediaries distribute them, so they are an emerging but still small cross-border option.
sources: RBA, Card costs and surcharging conclusions 2026
AusPayNet, Guide to high value payments

SGD.name: Singapore
SGD.line: A central bank that runs the real-time gross settlement system, lets licensed nonbanks connect directly to the instant rails, and links its PayNow instant service abroad one country at a time while building Nexus, a hub to link many.

dom: The Monetary Authority of Singapore is central bank and single regulator. It licenses payment firms under the Payment Services Act and designates systemically important systems. Bank industry bodies write the scheme rules, and the new Singapore Payments Network is taking over governance of the national schemes.
Association of Banks in Singapore, Singapore Clearing House Association, Singapore Payments Network

Banks and licensed payment institutions send SGD instantly over FAST, the instant payment system, and over PayNow, its overlay that uses a phone number or company ID. GIRO carries batch payroll and bill payments. Major payment institutions such as e-wallets can connect directly to FAST and PayNow.
Banks hold customer deposits. Licensed payment institutions hold e-wallet balances and must safeguard customer funds, usually at a bank.

MAS runs MEPS+, the real-time gross settlement system where direct participants settle large-value payments in central bank money. Banking Computer Services, a NETS subsidiary, operates FAST and PayNow. Retail clearing produces net positions that settle across participants' accounts at MAS, as is normal for deferred net settlement systems.

MAS oversees designated systems against international standards for financial market infrastructures and supervises banks and payment institutions. Each licensed firm owns its own compliance and customer obligations.
xb: MAS sets cross-border licensing under the Payment Services Act and agrees each PayNow link with the partner central bank. Nexus Global Payments, owned by the participating central banks, will set the rules for Nexus, a planned hub linking many countries' instant payment systems.
Bank of Thailand, Reserve Bank of India, Bank Negara Malaysia

Most cross-border value moves through correspondent banking, with Singapore acting as a regional hub. Remittance firms and global payment companies licensed as payment institutions handle smaller flows. PayNow links to Thailand's PromptPay, India's UPI and Malaysia's DuitNow carry person-to-person transfers using a phone number.

Correspondent banks hold nostro and vostro balances for foreign banks. On instant links, participants or link operators hold prefunded or settlement balances in each currency, as bilateral links normally work.
Banks and e-wallets in each country

Each leg settles in its home system, with the SGD leg in MEPS+, the real-time gross settlement system, and FX settling through CLS or the correspondent's books. Nexus is planned with a NETS and PayNet venture as technical operator, and will link FAST to other instant systems through one connection.
MAS supervises the Singapore side and each partner regulator supervises its own. Sending and receiving institutions own anti-money laundering screening and remittance rules on their leg.
Monetary Authority of Singapore and partner central banks

SGD.stablecoin: MAS has a framework for single-currency stablecoins pegged to SGD or G10 currencies, with full reserves and par redemption earning a MAS-regulated label. A recent consultation proposes putting it into the Payment Services Act with an issuance licence, making regulated stablecoins a defined option for cross-border settlement.
sources: MAS Nonbank access to FAST and PayNow

HKD.name: Hong Kong
HKD.line: One clearing house runs real-time gross settlement in four currencies, with commercial banks as settlement institutions for US dollars, euros and renminbi while the HKMA settles Hong Kong dollars.

dom: The HKMA licenses banks and e-wallet (stored value) operators and designates and oversees payment systems under the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance. It applies international standards for financial market infrastructures to the systems it oversees.

Banks and licensed e-wallet (stored value) operators move payments for customers. Instant retail transfers run on FPS, the Faster Payment System, which connects banks and wallets around the clock using phone numbers, email addresses or QR codes.

Banks hold customer deposits and e-wallet operators hold customer float. Three commercial banks issue Hong Kong dollar banknotes, backed by US dollars paid into the Exchange Fund at a fixed rate of HK$7.80 to US$1.
HSBC, Bank of China (Hong Kong), Standard Chartered Hong Kong

Hong Kong Interbank Clearing Limited, jointly owned by the HKMA and the Hong Kong Association of Banks, operates HKD CHATS, the real-time gross settlement system, and FPS, the instant payment system. Banks settle in real time across their settlement accounts at the HKMA. Wallet operators settle through a bank they appoint as settlement participant.

Each bank and wallet operator owns its customer relationship, fraud controls and safeguarding of funds. The HKMA supervises them and gives designated systems statutory settlement finality, so a settled payment cannot be unwound on insolvency.
xb: The HKMA appoints the settlement institutions for foreign currency clearing and agrees cross-border links with other central banks, such as the People's Bank of China and the Bank of Thailand.
People's Bank of China, Bank of Thailand

Most cross-border flows run through correspondent banking. FPS, Hong Kong's instant payment system, also links to Thailand's PromptPay for QR payments and to mainland China's IBPS instant system through Payment Connect for small remittances.
HSBC, Standard Chartered, Bank of China (Hong Kong)

Banks hold foreign currency balances in Hong Kong with the appointed settlement institution, and with correspondents in the currency's home market. Renminbi liquidity sits with the RMB clearing bank, which links back to the mainland clearing system.

USD, EUR and RMB CHATS settle in real time on the books of the appointed commercial bank rather than the HKMA. The four CHATS systems are linked so FX trades settle payment-versus-payment, and CLS, the FX settlement system, is a designated system. The HKMA is a founding member of mBridge, a platform shared by several central banks for settlement in digital currency.
USD CHATS, EUR CHATS, RMB CHATS

The sending bank owns sanctions screening and compliance for its customers. Settlement institutions carry the foreign currency settlement role under HKMA appointment and oversight, and partner central banks jointly oversee each fast payment link.

HKD.stablecoin: Issuing fiat-referenced stablecoins in Hong Kong requires an HKMA licence under the Stablecoins Ordinance. The first licences went to HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial, which makes licensed stablecoins an emerging cross-border option alongside correspondent banking.

BRL.name: Brazil
BRL.line: The central bank builds, owns and runs the core rails itself, both the STR system that settles large payments one by one and the Pix instant system, and lets payment institutions plug into them directly.

dom: Banco Central do Brasil regulates and oversees payment schemes, payment institutions and payment systems under National Monetary Council guidelines. It also created the Pix instant payment scheme and writes its rules. Card networks set rules for their own schemes with central bank authorization.
Banco Central do Brasil, National Monetary Council

Banks, payment institutions and credit unions send Pix instant payments, TED bank transfers and card payments for customers. Larger participants connect to Pix directly, and most smaller ones connect through a direct participant.
Itaú Unibanco, Banco do Brasil, Bradesco

Customer funds sit in deposit accounts at banks and in payment accounts at payment institutions. Banks hold reserve accounts at the central bank, while payment institutions and payment systems can hold settlement accounts there. Direct Pix participants also hold a dedicated instant payment account at the central bank.
Reserve, settlement and instant payment accounts

The central bank operates STR, which settles large transfers one by one with finality and no overdraft. Pix payments settle individually, 24 hours a day, in SPI, a second central bank system that uses the instant payment accounts. Card and other retail flows are netted by private clearing providers, with net positions settled in central bank accounts.

The central bank authorizes and supervises institutions and oversees the payment systems. Commercial banks must join SPI, the Pix settlement system, directly, and large institutions must offer Pix. Each institution owns its own compliance, and a direct participant carries settlement for the indirect participants it sponsors.
xb: Brazil's foreign exchange law gives the central bank power to regulate the FX market and authorize who operates in it. Central bank rules set the details, including those for international payment services known as eFX.

Only institutions authorized by the central bank may carry out FX operations. Banks handle most flows through correspondent relationships, and authorized eFX providers offer international payment and transfer services to their own clients with a contracted foreign counterpart.
Itaú Unibanco, Banco do Brasil, Bradesco

Foreign banks hold BRL accounts at authorized Brazilian banks, and those banks can process BRL payment orders to and from abroad through them. Brazilian banks hold foreign currency with correspondents abroad.

The BRL leg of an FX operation settles domestically through the banks and STR, the central bank's large-value system, and the foreign leg settles in correspondent accounts abroad. eFX payments with foreign counterparts must run through an FX operation or a non-resident BRL account, with no netting.

The authorized institution must identify the client, sender and recipient and apply anti-money laundering controls. Banks must assess each foreign institution that holds a BRL account with them. The central bank authorizes and supervises FX institutions and eFX providers.

BRL.stablecoin: Central bank rules now place virtual asset services, including international transfers and buying or selling fiat-pegged tokens, inside the FX market rules, so stablecoin cross-border payments run through authorized providers as FX operations. eFX providers may not settle with virtual assets, though stablecoins remain usable in the wider FX market.
sources: BCB, The role of the Banco Central do Brasil
BCB, Centralized settlement of card arrangements

INR.name: India
INR.line: A bank-owned national utility runs the retail rails while consumer apps that hold no money front most payments, with banks keeping the accounts and the central bank settling everything in rupees.

dom: The Reserve Bank of India authorises and oversees every payment system under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act. System operators then write the scheme rules for their own rails, with NPCI, the bank-owned national payments utility, setting the participation and liability rules for UPI, the instant payment system.

Banks send large payments through the Reserve Bank's real-time gross settlement system and smaller transfers through NEFT, its batch system. NPCI routes retail payments over UPI and IMPS for instant transfers, NACH for bulk payments and the RuPay card network. Third-party apps such as PhonePe, Google Pay and Paytm plug into UPI only through a sponsor bank, and payment aggregators collect for merchants.

Customer funds sit in bank accounts, and UPI apps only link to them. Non-bank prepaid wallet issuers and payment aggregators must keep customer and merchant money in an escrow account at a scheduled commercial bank.
State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank

The Reserve Bank operates its real-time gross settlement system and NEFT, which settles in batches, both around the clock. NPCI acts as clearing house for UPI and its other retail systems, netting each bank's position and settling it in the bank's settlement account at the Reserve Bank in several cycles a day.
Real-time gross settlement and NEFT operator

The Reserve Bank holds overall responsibility as regulator and overseer of payment systems. NPCI, the retail scheme operator, audits its participants, sponsor banks answer for the apps they onboard, and the app is the first point of contact for customer complaints.
xb: The Reserve Bank sets cross-border rules under the Foreign Exchange Management Act and the payments law. It authorises overseas money transfer operators and cross-border payment aggregators, and approves rupee vostro arrangements for foreign correspondent banks.

Authorised dealer banks move most flows over Swift through correspondent banking. Inward remittances also arrive through foreign exchange houses with rupee drawing arrangements and money transfer operators with Indian agents, and NPCI International links UPI, India's instant payment system, to foreign fast payment systems such as Singapore's PayNow.
State Bank of India, ICICI Bank

Authorised dealer banks hold foreign currency nostro accounts abroad and rupee vostro accounts for foreign banks and exchange houses at home. Cross-border payment aggregators keep separate inward and outward collection accounts at authorised dealer banks.
State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank

Foreign currency legs settle on the books of correspondent banks abroad, while the rupee leg reaches the beneficiary over domestic rails, from real-time gross settlement and NEFT batch transfers to IMPS and UPI instant payments. Remittance payouts must land in a bank account or a capped prepaid card rather than cash for larger sums.
Reserve Bank of India for the rupee leg

The Reserve Bank oversees cross-border operators and foreign exchange compliance. Authorised dealer banks carry the reporting and customer due diligence for each flow, and payment aggregators supply the documents banks need to close export and import records.

INR.stablecoin: Stablecoins have no payments framework in India and the Reserve Bank has publicly argued against them, pointing to UPI links and central bank digital currency corridors as its preferred cross-border routes. A retail e-rupee pilot is running.
sources: NPCI, Guidelines for TPAPs in UPI
Roles of NPCI, PSP and TPAP in UPI
RBI, Master Direction on Payment Aggregators
RBI, FAQ on RDA and MTSS
Business Standard, RBI DG on stablecoins

AUD.rails_owner_note: Industry bodies owned by the banks run the main rails, while the Reserve Bank runs RITS, the system where they all settle.
AUD.nonbank_note: Licensed nonbank payment providers that need to settle with other providers can apply for their own settlement account at the Reserve Bank, and some already hold one.
sources: AusPayNet, Guide to high value payments
East and Partners, Wise first nonbank settlement account

BRL.rails_owner_note: The central bank owns and runs the two core rails, Pix for instant payments and STR for large transfers.
BRL.nonbank_note: Authorized payment institutions can hold their own accounts at the central bank and join Pix settlement directly, and large ones do.
sources: BCB, The role of the Banco Central do Brasil

CAD.rails_owner_note: Payments Canada, whose members are financial institutions, runs the core systems and the bank-owned Interac runs debit and e-Transfer, with everything settling at the Bank of Canada.
CAD.nonbank_note: Payment companies supervised by the Bank of Canada can now join Payments Canada and qualify for a settlement account for the new Real-Time Rail, as the rail switches on in phases.
sources: Bank of Canada, settlement account policy for the Real-Time Rail
Bank of Canada, Overview of Lynx

EUR.rails_owner_note: The Eurosystem runs T2 and TIPS, while EBA Clearing, owned by banks, runs the largest clearing systems for bulk and instant payments.
EUR.nonbank_note: Licensed payment and e-money firms are now allowed to hold settlement-only accounts in T2 and TIPS, but few have joined so far.
sources: Eurosystem policy on nonbank payment provider access

GBP.rails_owner_note: The Bank of England runs CHAPS for high-value payments, while Pay.UK, the industry-funded operator, runs Faster Payments and Bacs.
GBP.nonbank_note: Authorised payment and e-money firms can hold their own settlement account at the Bank of England, and several do.
sources: BoE, nonbank payment provider access to settlement accounts

HKD.rails_owner_note: The HKMA sets up the rails and settles Hong Kong dollars on its own books, and Hong Kong Interbank Clearing, a company it owns jointly with the banks' association, runs them day to day.
HKD.nonbank_note: Licensed e-wallet operators can join FPS for clearing only and must settle through a bank they appoint.

INR.rails_owner_note: The Reserve Bank runs the large-value and batch transfer systems, while NPCI, owned by banks, runs UPI and the other retail rails.
INR.nonbank_note: The Reserve Bank allows some nonbank payment firms, such as wallet issuers and card networks, to join its central systems directly with their own current account, but most nonbanks still settle through banks.
sources: RBI, FAQ on nonbank access to central payment systems

SGD.rails_owner_note: The Monetary Authority of Singapore runs MEPS+ for large payments, while bank bodies govern FAST, PayNow and GIRO and a NETS subsidiary operates them.
SGD.nonbank_note: Major payment institutions can connect directly to FAST and PayNow, but central bank settlement accounts in MEPS+ remain with banks and market infrastructures.
sources: MAS, nonbank access to FAST and PayNow

rails.name: ACH
rails.owner: The Fed and The Clearing House

USD.rails_owner_note: The Fed runs Fedwire, FedNow and its own ACH operator side by side with The Clearing House, owned by large banks, which runs CHIPS, RTP and the other ACH operator.
USD.nonbank_note: Only institutions the law makes eligible, mostly banks and credit unions, can hold a Fed account, and the proposed payment account keeps that eligibility, so fintechs settle through sponsor banks.
sources: Morrison Foerster, Fed payment account proposal

CAD.obs: Payment companies are getting their own seat
CAD.take: With Real-Time Rail a registered payment company can hold its own settlement account at the Bank of Canada. It still tops that account up through a bank, but no longer settles through one.

USD.obs: Two sets of rails run side by side
USD.take: What a bank can reach depends on which rails it joins, the Fed's or the big banks', and both settle on Fed accounts.

GBP.obs: A payment company can skip the bank
GBP.take: In the UK a regulated payment company can settle at the Bank of England itself, which many countries still don't allow.

EUR.take: Within SEPA a payment to another euro country runs on the same rails and rules as a local one, with no correspondent in the middle.

AUD.obs: Every fast payment settles on its own, at any hour
AUD.take: The Reserve Bank settles each NPP payment one by one, around the clock, in central bank money. Payroll and direct debits still run in batches on BECS.

SGD.obs: Links are built one country at a time
SGD.take: PayNow connects to neighbours through separate bilateral links. Nexus is meant to replace many links with one hub.

HKD.take: Hong Kong dollars settle at the HKMA. US dollars, euros and renminbi settle on the books of commercial banks appointed to do that job, so those payments never reach the HKMA.

BRL.obs: The central bank runs the rail and settles it
BRL.take: Pix is built, owned and run by the central bank, so no separate industry operator sits between participants and settlement.

rows.label: A Pix payment
nodes: Pix, run by the central bank

INR.obs: The app owns the customer, the bank holds the money
INR.take: UPI apps sit in front, but the money sits in bank accounts, and banks settle the totals between them at the Reserve Bank.

6.take: How the money lands decides who holds it at the end.
why: This is the far end of a payment from abroad. A wallet balance is a claim on the wallet operator, a bank credit is a deposit, and cash ends the chain. The partner that pays out is often settled in bulk later, so it may be owed the money it has just handed over.
know: Payout partners are usually settled in bulk, not payment by payment. Either the sender places money with the agent in advance or the agent pays first and is repaid at the next settlement, and whoever pays first is exposed until then.
India allows cash payout of inbound transfers only up to a set limit. Larger amounts must land in a bank account, which moves the last holder from an agent to a bank.
Payout from a global company is usually a local payment from a balance already in the country, so the recipient's side sees a domestic transfer that is final under local rules.
second_head: The same payment from abroad can end as a wallet balance, cash at a counter or a credit to a local account, and each one has a different holder.

5.take: Fast money across a border is paid out of a balance that was already there.
why: This layer appears only when a payment changes currency. It sets the rate, carries the exchange risk and pays the cost of keeping money ready in the receiving country before anyone asks for it.
know: Global payment companies keep balances in many currencies at local banks or central banks, pay out from them and rebalance in bulk. A transfer that looks instant rarely crosses the border at that moment.
About a tenth of foreign exchange settlement still runs one side at a time with no protection, so one party can pay and never receive. About a third settles both sides together, mostly through CLS.

Where both currency legs settle together, in CLS or a similar payment versus payment system, neither side pays before the other. Outside that, the party that pays first carries the risk until the other leg lands.
second_head: Money comes in on one side, the provider converts it on its own books, and a balance on the other side pays out now.

4.take: The network carries the message and writes the rules. It holds no money.
why: Card networks, instant payment schemes and Swift decide who can send what and carry the instruction between banks. Processors run the card and account software underneath for whoever holds the licence. Both reach across every other layer without ever holding a balance.
know: Visa and Mastercard hold no card payments, yet each promises to cover a client that fails to pay its settlement to other clients. Visa's largest daily settlement exposure runs many times larger than the collateral it holds.

The instant rail runs nonstop but the settlement behind it may not. Faster Payments credits customers around the clock while banks settle three times a business day, and UPI settles in ten cycles a day.
A processor runs the balance and the statement, but the licence, the customer money and the duty to regulators stay with the bank or licensed firm that hired it.
second_head: Two banks, a network between them and a processor underneath. The instruction travels on this layer. The money moves on the ones below it.

3.take: One company with local accounts in many countries. The money mostly stays inside each one.
why: This is the layer that makes a cross-border payment look domestic at both ends. The company collects into its own account in one country and pays out from its own account in another, so no correspondent bank sits in the middle.
know: Some of these companies hold their own settlement accounts and connect directly to instant systems. Wise reports direct access in the UK, the EU through Hungary, Singapore, Australia, Brazil and the Philippines.
Each local entity safeguards customer money under its own licence, so the same balance can be protected differently depending on which entity holds it.

Nothing crosses the border when a customer pays in. The money lands in the company's local account and is final under that country's domestic rules. The company moves value between its own entities later, in bulk.
second_head: A customer pays into a local account, the company settles between its own entities, and a local account on the far side pays the recipient.

2.take: The bank holds the money and answers for it, whatever name is on the app.
why: Banks appear twice in a payment. As correspondents they hold accounts for other banks and move money across borders one book transfer at a time. As sponsors they hold the funds and the central bank account for apps and smaller institutions that have neither.
know: When a fintech sends batch payments through a sponsor bank, the payment system sees only the bank. Under US batch rules the bank gives warranties to every receiving bank for each item it sends, whatever the fintech promised its own customers.
A correspondent payment is a series of separate book transfers, each final in one bank's books before the next starts. No single system ties the hops together the way a domestic system does.
Many smaller institutions settle through a settlement agent's central bank account rather than their own. Exposure gathers in a few agents, and system operators are expected to watch that tiering.
second_head: How far banks sit from the central bank
Banks sit on the first ring, next to the central bank. Everything further out settles through one of them.

1.take: A payment is final when the central bank's ledger says so, not when the app does.
why: Every other layer ends here. The central bank holds the settlement accounts, and finality law means a payment settled on its books stays settled even if a participant becomes insolvent afterwards.
know: Finality is a legal status granted to a designated system, not a property of fast software. The system's own rules set the exact moment a payment can no longer be revoked.
Many private systems become final only when the central bank books their totals. The Federal Reserve's National Settlement Service posts net results from clearing houses straight to member accounts.
Batch systems wait for central bank hours. US batch payments settle four times a business day and wait over weekends and holidays, while instant systems keep settling.
second_head: Instant systems run around the clock. Wires and batch payments settle only while the central bank's settlement service is open.

CAD.note: Each wire settles on its own at the Bank of Canada once the sender has the liquidity, and the recipient is credited after that.
Items are credited ahead of settlement. Net positions settle across Bank of Canada accounts the next business day, and surviving clearers share the loss if one cannot pay.
The recipient is credited at once. Institutions settle with each other through Lynx the next business day, up to four days over a weekend, with no collateral and no guarantee from Interac.
Planned. A payment settles only once funds in the sender's settlement account are reserved, and a completed transfer is final and irrevocable.

USD.note: Each wire is final when the Federal Reserve records it, drawing on intraday credit against the bank's cap if needed.
Settles one at a time in a Federal Reserve master account around the clock, with no prefunding required. Final when the debit and credit are recorded.
Settles four times a business day and not on weekends or holidays. An unauthorised consumer debit can still be returned within 60 days of settlement.
A payment releases only when covered by funds in the prefunded account at the New York Fed, and each released payment is final at once.
Each payment is covered by funds already in a joint account at the New York Fed and is final when released. The central bank holds the money and the operator keeps the ledger.

GBP.note: Each payment settles individually in the Bank of England's settlement service, with offsetting non-urgent payments matched every few minutes to save liquidity.
Credited at once around the clock. Banks settle net three times a business day against cash set aside at the Bank of England.
A three-day cycle. Receiving accounts are credited early on day three and net positions settle at the Bank of England later that morning, inside each participant's debit cap.
Authorisation is a promise, not a payment. Net positions usually settle the next business day, and chargeback rights run for months after.

EUR.note: Each payment settles individually at the national central bank, Monday to Friday only.
Bulk payments are netted and the net amounts settle in T2 during the business day. Nothing settles at weekends while T2 is closed.
Final within seconds under the scheme rules. RT1 settles in central bank funds through TIPS, so the money behind it sits at the Eurosystem.
The amount is reserved, the payee's bank accepts, and settlement is final within the ten second limit the regulation sets.

AUD.note: Each payment settles on its own from the bank's Fast Settlement Service slice of its settlement account, at any hour, and cannot be recalled.
Files are exchanged bilaterally and netted into five settlement windows through the day, with a late evening exchange settling the next morning.
Swift messages between banks, settled one by one in RITS across Exchange Settlement Accounts.
The cardholder sees the purchase at once. Card obligations are netted and settled in batches through the Low Value Settlement Service.

SGD.note: The payee is credited first. Net files go to MEPS+ in set cycles each business day, and each bank's net outflow must be covered by collateral at the central bank.
Each large payment settles individually at the Monetary Authority of Singapore, with collateralised intraday liquidity and gridlock resolution.
Batch payroll and bill payments, netted and settled across accounts at the Monetary Authority on a daily cycle.

HKD.note: Settles one by one on the HKMA's books, with free secured intraday liquidity and an optimiser that offsets queued payments every half hour.
Each payment settles individually from the bank's FPS ledger, which is swept from its main settlement ledger, around the clock.

BRL.note: Settles in the sender's instant payment account at the central bank within seconds. A fraud claim can still pull back what remains in the receiving account for up to 80 days.
Large transfers settle one by one at the central bank with no overdraft, during its business day window.
Retail and card flows are netted by the private clearing provider and the net positions settle in central bank accounts.
Authorisation is a promise. Net positions settle later in central bank accounts, and merchant receivables are registered centrally so they can be pledged before they are paid.

INR.note: Credited at once. NPCI nets each bank's position and settles it at the Reserve Bank in ten cycles a day, with a guarantee fund behind a bank that cannot pay.
Runs around the clock. Each transfer settles individually at the Reserve Bank and the receiving bank credits the customer soon after.
Transfers are batched and settled in frequent cycles around the clock at the Reserve Bank.
Bulk debits and credits are netted by NPCI as clearing house and the net positions settle in the banks' accounts at the Reserve Bank in cycles.

CAD.note: Direct Lynx participant with its own settlement account, funded by pledged collateral.
Never touches the central bank directly. Its central is the Lynx participant and must prefund the wires its members send.
Holds customer funds in trust or an insured account at a bank or trust company and settles everything through it.
