Planned. A supervised payment company can hold its own settlement account for the Real-Time Rail, but still tops it up through a Lynx participant.
The app keeps the record of who owns what. The sponsor holds the money and the seat.

USD.note: Holds a master account and can run a daylight overdraft against its cap.

chain: Bankers' bank or corporate credit union
USD.note: Can settle FedNow payments inside its correspondent's master account instead of holding the liquidity itself.
Customer money sits in a pooled account at the sponsor. The app's records decide whether each customer is insured.
A middleware firm keeps the sub-ledger between the app and the bank. It holds no money and adds a record that must match the bank's.
No non-bank holds a Fed account, so even a licensed transmitter settles through a bank.

GBP.note: Reserves account, intraday liquidity and a direct link to CHAPS and Faster Payments.

GBP.who: Licensed payment company with a settlement account
GBP.note: Holds a settlement account but no reserves account, so it funds every payment from cash placed there in advance and gets no credit from the Bank.
Has its own link to the Faster Payments scheme, but a sponsor's account is where the money lands.
The sponsor manages both the connection and the settlement.
Customer money sits in a segregated safeguarding account at a bank. It is a claim on the app, not a deposit.

EUR.note: Holds a T2 account at its national central bank. Instant payment liquidity on a TIPS account counts as reserves.

EUR.who: Licensed payment company with a central bank account
EUR.note: Allowed a settlement-only account in T2 or TIPS with a capped balance and no intraday credit. Few have joined so far.
Most still safeguard customer money at a bank and settle through it.

EUR.who: Smaller bank in a clearing house
EUR.note: Settles through another direct participant's cash account, with that participant's prior approval.
The balance is a claim on the app, safeguarded at a bank, and not covered by deposit insurance.

AUD.note: Holds an Exchange Settlement Account split into a slice for instant payments and a slice for everything else.
Below the threshold for its own account it settles high-value payments through an agent and can keep a dormant account in reserve.
Offers instant payments through a sponsor and settles in the sponsor's account.

AUD.who: Licensed non-bank with a settlement account
AUD.note: Can hold its own account, yet still needs a licensed bank to clear and settle its instant payments.
Links directly to start payments but does not clear or settle.

SGD.note: Direct MEPS+ participant. Posts collateral at the central bank to cover its net outflow on FAST.
Connects to FAST and PayNow itself but settles through a bank, whose collateral must also cover the non-bank's position.
Holds customer money at a bank under a trust account or a bank undertaking.
Holds a balance at a member bank in each country it serves, on terms agreed outside the scheme.

HKD.note: Holds an RTGS ledger and an FPS ledger that sweep between each other.
Joins FPS for clearing only and settles through a bank it appoints.

chain: Bank of China (Hong Kong), the clearing bank
HKD.note: Renminbi settles on the clearing bank's books, which link back to the mainland system.
Holds Hong Kong dollars at a correspondent that holds the settlement account.

BRL.note: Reserve account plus a dedicated instant payment account. Must join Pix settlement directly.
Direct Pix participant with its own instant payment account. Customer balances are backed one for one by central bank cash or short government bonds.

BRL.who: Small credit union or payment institution
BRL.note: Most indirect participants connect through a direct participant that acts as their settlement institution.

BRL.who: Payment firm without a central bank licence
BRL.note: Can only take part in Pix indirectly.
Starts a Pix from an account held elsewhere and never holds the money.

INR.note: Settles UPI nets from its own real-time gross settlement account, which NPCI is allowed to debit.
Holds no money. The customer's funds stay in a bank account and the app's handle resolves at its sponsor bank.
Customer money sits in an escrow account at a commercial bank.
Merchant money sits in escrow at a bank until it is paid out.

INR.who: Card network with a central bank account
INR.note: Some non-banks, such as card networks and wallet issuers, may hold a current account at the Reserve Bank, but most still settle through banks.

failures.label: Sent to the wrong person or scammed
failures.line: The sending firm acts first, and in most countries the customer carries the loss of a scam they authorised unless a local rule moves it to the firms.
differs: GBP
The sending firm reimburses within five business days up to a cap per claim, and the receiving firm pays back half.
BRL
The receiving institution blocks and returns what is still in the account, so recovery is limited to the available balance.
EUR
Agreed rules, not yet in force, will require a refund when a fraudster impersonates the customer's own bank.
SGD
For phishing that leads to unauthorised transfers, the bank pays if it missed a duty, then the telecoms operator, otherwise the customer.
AUD
No general reimbursement rule. A firm compensates only where it broke a framework duty and that failure caused the loss.
USD
No general reimbursement rule for a transfer the customer sent personally. Federal liability tiers apply only to unauthorised transfers.

failures.label: Card is disputed
failures.line: The issuer raises the dispute, the network's rules decide it, and the merchant usually bears the loss, with the acquirer paying if the merchant cannot.
differs: AUD
About nine in ten debit cards carry two networks, so which scheme's dispute rules apply depends on how the acquirer routed the payment.
INR
Only the issuer and the network may store the card number, so saved-card payments run on tokens they hold rather than on a merchant's own store.
BRL
Merchant card receivables are registered centrally and can be pledged to a lender that is not the acquirer before they are paid.
CAD
Debit card fraud protection is a voluntary industry code covering PIN debit at terminals, not a regulation.
USD
Federal law sets tiers for consumer liability on unauthorised debit transfers, and the issuing bank, not the fintech brand on the card, is the covered party.

failures.label: App or payment company goes bust
failures.line: Customers are repaid from the money the firm was required to set aside, through an insolvency process, and deposit insurance usually does not apply.
differs: GBP
Safeguarded funds are kept apart from the firm's own assets, and a resolution pack is meant to help an administrator return them quickly.
EUR
The balance is a claim on the firm and not a deposit, so deposit insurance does not apply.
USD
The money usually sits at a partner bank. Insurance passes through to each customer only for a bank failure and only if records show whose money is whose.
INR
Wallet and payment aggregator funds sit in escrow at a scheduled commercial bank.
BRL
Payment account funds are outside the firm's bankruptcy by law, and e-money issuers hold them at the central bank or in federal government bonds.
CAD
A payment company must hold end-user funds in a trust account or an insured separate account, with a direct relationship to the bank that holds them.
SGD
A major payment institution must safeguard customer money by the end of the next business day, in a trust account or under a bank undertaking.

failures.label: A bank fails
failures.line: The deposit insurer repays insured depositors, and finality law stops payments already settled from being unwound.
differs: GBP
Faster Payments and Bacs complete settlement from cash the failed bank set aside at the Bank of England.
EUR
EURO1 completes settlement through a liquidity pool and loss sharing among members.
CAD
Lynx leaves no exposure between participants. In the batch system ACSS the surviving clearers share the shortfall.
INR
A settlement guarantee fund, mostly a credit line NPCI arranges from banks, pays so the UPI cycle completes, and the surviving banks of that cycle bear a permanent loss.
USD
Pass-through insurance protects app customers only if the app's records pass the FDIC's tests.
SGD
Each bank's collateral at the central bank must cover its net outflow on FAST, including for the non-banks it settles for.

failures.label: A system goes down
failures.line: The operator restores service and completes settlement, while banks and their customers usually absorb the delay because operator rules limit the operator's liability.
differs: USD
FedNow's rules exclude the Reserve Banks' liability for problems beyond their reasonable control, and CHIPS participants can fall back on Fedwire.
CAD
Payments Canada and the Bank of Canada are not liable to members for losses from good-faith acts under the Real-Time Rail by-law.
BRL
The central bank runs Pix itself, so it carries the recovery duty directly.
AUD
The Reserve Bank runs the settlement system, and a fast payment is rejected rather than queued when a bank's instant payment slice runs short.
EUR
If no confirmation arrives within ten seconds on an instant payment, the paying provider must restore the payer's account.

standout.obs: Seen in seconds. Settled next day, uncovered.
standout.take: Interac e-Transfer credits the recipient at once, but the institutions settle with each other through Lynx the next business day and up to four days later over a weekend. Interac does not move the funds, guarantee settlement or hold collateral, so the sending institution owes the receiving one until then.

data.note: Each wire settles on its own at the Bank of Canada once the sender has the liquidity, and the recipient is credited after that.
Items are credited ahead of settlement. Net positions settle across Bank of Canada accounts the next business day, and surviving clearers share the loss if one cannot pay.
The recipient is credited at once. Institutions settle with each other through Lynx the next business day, up to four days over a weekend, with no collateral and no guarantee from Interac.
Planned. A payment settles only once funds in the sender's settlement account are reserved, and a completed transfer is final and irrevocable.

notice.t: Two loss rules under one bank
notice.d: Lynx settles each wire only when the sender has the liquidity, so participants carry no exposure to each other. In the batch system ACSS the surviving clearers must cover a defaulter's net debit.

notice.t: Credit unions reach the rails through a central
notice.d: Central 1 is the Lynx participant for most credit unions and must prefund the wires its members send. The central a credit union belongs to sets its cut-offs and funding burden.

notice.t: Customer funds must sit directly at a bank
notice.d: A payment company holding end-user funds keeps them in a trust account or an insured separate account, with a direct relationship to the account provider. Funds held through another payment company's account are accepted only by exception.

notice.t: One settlement layer, more than one exchange
notice.d: Under the Real-Time Rail by-law a payment settles only once funds are reserved in the sender's account, and third-party exchanges that sign an agreement can submit settlement instructions.

notice.t: Cheques still carry about a fifth of value
notice.d: Paper items average about 8,000 dollars each against about 45 dollars for a debit card payment, and they clear through the batch system.

notice.t: Debit fraud protection is a voluntary code
notice.d: The code covers PIN debit at terminals and cash machines. Cardholders are not liable for issuer errors or use after a loss is reported, and transactions outside Canada are out of scope.

standout.obs: One pooled account. Owners on the app's books.
standout.take: A fintech's customer money usually sits in one pooled custodial account at a partner bank. Deposit insurance reaches each customer only if records show whose money is whose, and today those records can sit with the fintech or its ledger provider rather than with the bank.

data.bank: One pooled account in the fintech's name, held for its customers
data.app: A row per customer, with name and balance
data.link: The rows must add up to the pooled balance

notice.t: Two instant rails, two funding models
notice.d: FedNow settles in a bank's master account with no prefunding, drawing on the same intraday credit as Fedwire. RTP settles from a joint account at the New York Fed that participants fill in advance.

notice.t: FedNow without a bank's own Fed liquidity
notice.d: An institution can settle its FedNow payments inside a correspondent's master account, such as a bankers' bank or corporate credit union, so the correspondent holds the liquidity.

notice.t: No sending or receiving until funded
notice.d: A CHIPS participant cannot send or receive until it funds its opening position at the New York Fed. Each dollar of funding settles about 26 dollars of payments, and payments still unsettled at day end are deleted.

notice.t: The originating bank stands behind ACH debits for years
notice.d: A consumer's bank can return an unauthorised debit within about 60 days, and can bring a warranty claim against the originating bank for entries up to two years old. A sponsor bank carries that risk for its originators.

notice.t: The sponsor bank's size sets the card economics
notice.d: Issuers under 10 billion dollars in assets are exempt from the debit interchange cap, so a fintech debit program inherits its issuing bank's economics. The routing rules apply to every issuer.

notice.t: Zelle messages now and settles over ACH or RTP
notice.d: The recipient sees the money within minutes while the two banks settle later through ACH or, when both are enabled, through RTP. Two Zelle payments can settle on different rails.

standout.obs: Own account at the Bank. Cash up front.
standout.take: An authorised payment or e-money firm can hold a settlement account at the Bank of England, but not a reserves account. It gets no intraday liquidity and funds every payment from cash placed there in advance, which is what direct access costs.

data.note: Reserves account, intraday liquidity and a direct link to CHAPS and Faster Payments.

data.who: Licensed payment company with a settlement account
data.note: Holds a settlement account but no reserves account, so it funds every payment from cash placed there in advance and gets no credit from the Bank.
Has its own link to the Faster Payments scheme, but a sponsor's account is where the money lands.
The sponsor manages both the connection and the settlement.
Customer money sits in a segregated safeguarding account at a bank. It is a claim on the app, not a deposit.

notice.t: Sender repays the scam victim, receiver pays half
notice.d: For authorised push payment fraud over Faster Payments and CHAPS the sending firm reimburses up to 85,000 pounds per claim, and the receiving firm pays the sending firm half within five business days.

notice.t: A card network owns the retail rails' central system
notice.d: Vocalink, a Mastercard company, provides the central infrastructure for Faster Payments and Bacs, while Pay.UK sets the rules and answers to the Bank of England.

notice.t: A pooled central bank account backs another ledger
notice.d: An omnibus account lets a system operator hold participants' funds in one account held on trust while it runs its own ledger, which must match the omnibus balance in full at all times.

notice.t: A Direct Debit refund comes from the payer's bank
notice.d: Under the Direct Debit Guarantee the payer gets a full and immediate refund from their own bank if an error is made, and the banks sort out the indemnity claim between themselves afterwards.

notice.t: No phone number directory, so a name check instead
notice.d: Paym, which looked up a payee from a mobile number, has closed. Person to person transfers run on sort code and account number, with Confirmation of Payee returning match, close match, no match or unavailable before the payer confirms.

notice.t: Safeguarding needs a daily reconciliation and a resolution pack
notice.d: Payment and e-money firms must reconcile safeguarded funds on every reconciliation day, keep a pack recording where the funds are held, and file a monthly return.

standout.obs: One currency. National ledgers underneath it.
standout.take: When a bank in one euro country pays a bank in another through T2, the accounts of their national central banks change. The Eurosystem nets those positions every day into one balance per national central bank against the European Central Bank, and all of them add up to zero.

hub: Balances net to zero every day

notice.t: T2 closes at weekends while TIPS keeps settling
notice.d: Liquidity can move between T2 and TIPS only while T2 is open, so instant payment balances received on a Saturday stay on the TIPS account until Monday.

notice.t: Where instant payment liquidity sits changes its reserve treatment
notice.d: Balances on a TIPS dedicated cash account count towards a bank's minimum reserves. Balances on an ancillary system account, held by a clearing house's settlement bank, do not.

notice.t: Domestic euro payments often stay in one clearing house
notice.d: The Bundesbank's SEPA clearer settles through a sub-account of a T2 cash account, and reaching other clearing houses through STEP2 is optional, so reach depends on which clearing houses a provider joins.

notice.t: EURO1 admits large banks and settles through defaults
notice.d: Each payment is checked against the sender's debit cap and the receiver's credit cap and is final once processed. A liquidity pool and loss sharing cover a failing participant, and admission needs own funds of at least 1.25 billion euro.

notice.t: Skip the name check and the provider refunds
notice.d: The payer's provider must offer a free check of the payee's name against the account identifier. If it fails to run the check correctly and a defective payment results, it refunds the payer and recovers from whichever provider caused the failure.

notice.t: Thirteen euro countries run cards only on global networks
notice.d: About 61 percent of euro area card payments are processed by international schemes and 39 percent by national schemes, and nine national schemes each operate in only one member state.

standout.obs: One account at the Reserve Bank. Two slices.
standout.take: Each bank splits its Exchange Settlement Account into a slice for the Fast Settlement Service and a slice for everything else. Instant payments settle only from the fast slice, trigger points move funds between the two, and when the main system closes overnight and at weekends everything moves to the fast slice.

notice.t: Direct entry is exchanged bilaterally then netted in windows
notice.d: Institutions swap direct entry files with each other and each sends the Reserve Bank its own net figure for every counterparty. Five settlements follow through the day and there is no central matching of the two sides' figures.

notice.t: Smaller banks reach central bank money through an agent
notice.d: A deposit-taker whose high-value payments are below a set share of the total can settle through an agent bank and keep a dormant account for use if the agent's service fails.

notice.t: Clearing on NPP still means being a licensed bank
notice.d: A non-bank can hold a settlement account and connect directly to start payments, yet only a licensed deposit-taker clears and settles on NPP, so the sponsor relationship is the real access route.

notice.t: PayTo keeps every agreement in one central register
notice.d: Pull payment mandates sit in a central database run by NPP Australia. The payer approves, pauses and cancels each one in their own bank's channel, and the collecting business's bank can see the record.

notice.t: A mistaken payment comes back on a reporting clock
notice.d: Reported within 10 business days, the funds come back if the account holds them. Between 10 business days and 7 months the receiving bank holds and returns them unless the recipient shows entitlement. After 7 months the recipient must agree.

notice.t: Nine in ten debit cards carry two networks
notice.d: A domestic debit payment can run on eftpos or on a global card network, and least-cost routing sends in-person transactions to the cheaper one. The merchant's acquirer, not the cardholder, shapes which network carries it.

standout.obs: Connects itself. Settles through a bank.
standout.take: A major payment institution can connect to FAST and PayNow directly, but central bank settlement accounts stay with banks. The bank that settles for it must hold collateral at the Monetary Authority covering the non-bank's net outflow as well as its own, and cannot send further payments once that cover runs out.

notice.t: Phishing losses follow a waterfall starting at the bank
notice.d: Where a victim entered credentials on a fake site and unauthorised transfers followed, the bank pays first if it missed a duty, the mobile operator second, and if no duty was missed there is no payout. Scams the victim authorised sit outside it.

notice.t: Non-bank FX firms in Nexus settle through a bank
notice.d: A foreign exchange provider that is not a member of a country's instant system holds an account at a settlement access provider, an existing member bank. A return is sent as a new payment with a new quote.

notice.t: Licence by activity, safeguarding above a threshold
notice.d: Firms are licensed by activity, including merchant acquiring and cross-border transfer. Above set monthly volumes a firm becomes a major payment institution and must safeguard customer money by the end of the next business day.

notice.t: One company is scheme, processor and acquirer for debit
notice.d: NETS runs the EFTPOS debit scheme, processes it and acquires for it, with the Singapore banks as participants and issuers. The scheme is designated alongside the instant rail.

notice.t: One QR label carries many payment schemes
notice.d: SGQR is a single label co-owned by the Monetary Authority and the media regulator, so a merchant displays one code for several schemes. A trial tested letting the merchant keep only one acquiring relationship as well.

notice.t: The settlement system also settles government bonds
notice.d: MEPS+ settles large payments and lets clients such as other central banks hold and settle Singapore Government Securities on a delivery versus payment basis, with collateralised intraday liquidity and gridlock resolution.

standout.obs: Agreed by central banks. Settled by two banks.
standout.take: On the QR payment link between Hong Kong and Thailand, the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation and Bangkok Bank act as the settlement banks. The two instant systems clear on their own sides, and the cross-border settlement rests on those two banks' books.

notice.t: Instant payments draw on a second swept ledger
notice.d: Each bank holds an RTGS ledger and an FPS ledger. Funds sweep between them at levels the bank sets, and when the main system closes the remaining balance moves to the FPS ledger to fund overnight and weekend payments.

notice.t: Defending the peg changes the pool banks settle from
notice.d: The total of banks' clearing balances at the HKMA is the Aggregate Balance. When the HKMA buys or sells US dollars at the edges of the peg, the balance rises or falls by the same amount.

notice.t: Intraday liquidity is free, secured and offset half-hourly
notice.d: Most intraday liquidity in Hong Kong dollar CHATS comes from an interest-free repo with the HKMA against Exchange Fund paper, and an optimiser offsets queued payments every 30 minutes.

notice.t: One phone number can point to several accounts
notice.d: A payee can link a mobile number or email to several accounts and nominate a default, so the receiving account can change without the payer knowing. Pull payment consent can begin in the merchant's own app.

standout.obs: A wallet balance, backed by central bank money.
standout.take: An issuer of electronic money must hold liquid assets equal to every customer balance, as cash in a dedicated account at the central bank or as short federal government bonds. A bank that issues e-money must hold the balance as cash at the central bank only, so a payment account balance is matched one for one by central bank money or sovereign debt rather than by bank deposits.

notice.t: Pix fraud returns follow the money across several accounts
notice.d: The payer's institution can open a return up to 80 days after a fraudulent Pix. The central bank's key directory notifies every institution holding later transfers, each blocks what is still there, and returns come only from available balance.

notice.t: Pix accounts can be funded only in business hours
notice.d: An institution can add or withdraw liquidity in its instant payment account only during the large-value system's window, so balances are positioned ahead of time and top-ups are largest on Fridays.

notice.t: Only the receiving side pays for Pix
notice.d: Direct participants pay one centavo for every ten Pix credited to them, set to recover cost only. The sender pays nothing and failed payments are free.

notice.t: A clearing house sits between banks on FX trades
notice.d: The real is not settled in CLS. Interbank foreign exchange trades clear through the B3 clearing house, which becomes counterparty to each trade, nets positions and moves the real leg through its own account at the central bank.

notice.t: Card receivables are registered centrally and can be pledged
notice.d: Receivables owed to merchants must sit in an authorised registry before a lender can discount them or take them as collateral, and the loan names the institution that receives their settlement.

notice.t: Initiators start a Pix from accounts held elsewhere
notice.d: Under Open Finance a payment initiation firm can start a Pix from the customer's account at another institution, including inside its own app after a one-time link. The money still leaves from the account holding institution.

standout.obs: Apps hold nothing. Handles resolve at a bank.
standout.take: Every UPI app works through at least one sponsor bank, and under the multi-bank model it can use several at once. A handle can be redirected to a different sponsor, which also makes that bank the app's acquiring bank. The customer's money never leaves a bank account, so the sponsor relationship is the real point of dependency.

data.note: Settles UPI nets from its own real-time gross settlement account, which NPCI is allowed to debit.
Holds no money. The customer's funds stay in a bank account and the app's handle resolves at its sponsor bank.
Customer money sits in an escrow account at a commercial bank.
Merchant money sits in escrow at a bank until it is paid out.

data.who: Card network with a central bank account
data.note: Some non-banks, such as card networks and wallet issuers, may hold a current account at the Reserve Bank, but most still settle through banks.

notice.t: UPI banks prefund settlement and share default losses
notice.d: Each member settles from its own Reserve Bank account and must keep enough balance for its net debit. A guarantee fund, about nine tenths of it a credit line NPCI arranges from banks, pays if a member cannot, and the surviving members of that cycle bear a permanent loss.

notice.t: One UPI app cannot exceed 30 percent of volume
notice.d: The cap is measured over a rolling three months, and both the app and its sponsor bank must make sure it is met, so the sponsor carries part of the compliance exposure.

notice.t: UPI Lite splits the money from the spendable balance
notice.d: The money stays with the user's bank in an escrow or pool account while the spendable balance sits on the device. Payments need no PIN and the issuing bank reconciles and settles them afterwards.

notice.t: Only issuers and networks may store card numbers
notice.d: No other entity in the card chain may store actual card data. Merchants keep the last four digits and use tokens for saved cards, and the card networks are responsible for making sure everyone complies.

notice.t: UPI has joined a one-connection hub
notice.d: The Reserve Bank has joined the Nexus project with the central banks of Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, so an operator connects once instead of building a link for each country.

notice.t: Zero merchant fees on UPI are set by law
notice.d: Banks and providers are barred from charging a merchant discount rate on UPI and RuPay debit, with the government reimbursing them through an incentive scheme. A bill before Parliament would let the government decide by notification which modes may carry a fee.

7: Own the customer relationship and the interface. Customer funds usually sit with a bank or licensed payment company underneath.
Embed payments and cards in software that businesses already use.
Collect money in one country for payout in another.
6: Wallets on the phone where the recipient keeps and spends the money.
Agent networks that pay out in cash.
5: Convert currencies and hold balances on the far side so payouts land already funded.
Specialist banks that supply liquidity in currencies few others cover.
4: Set the rules for card payments and clear them between issuers and acquirers.
Run a country's own debit, transfer or instant payment brand.
Carry payment instructions between banks across borders.
Back-end providers that run issuing and ledgers for whoever holds the licence.
Software that connects fintech programs to sponsor banks.
3: Hold licences and local accounts in many countries and pay out domestically.
Serve one region at scale, often with their own licences in each market.
Connect senders to local payout partners across many corridors.
2: Hold accounts for other banks and clear foreign currency for them.
Give fintech programs and indirect participants access to settlement and hold the funds.
Settle on behalf of member credit unions.
1: Provide the settlement asset, central bank money, and run or oversee the core systems.
Settle each payment individually and finally, in real time.
Settle retail payments in seconds, around the clock.
Net a batch of payments and settle once, often the next business day.
Private systems settling in central bank money
Bank-owned systems whose final settlement lands at the central bank.

FIT.7: Top layer. The money usually sits with a bank or licensed company below it.
FIT.6: Far end of a payment, on the receiving side.
FIT.5: Only in payments that cross a border, between the two currencies.
FIT.4a: Across all layers. Holds no money.
FIT.4b: Across all layers, behind the app. Holds no money.
FIT.3: Below the app, above the banks. Holds money under its own licences.
FIT.2a: Between banks, on the old cross-border chain.
FIT.2b: Right under the app, with its own account at the central bank.
FIT.1: Bottom layer. Once a payment lands here it is final.
